report.tagline: A free AI search tool that answers doctors' medical questions using trusted journals, with sources cited.
report.simpleSummary: OpenEvidence is like ChatGPT, but only for doctors and nurses. A doctor types a question, like 'best drug for this patient with kidney disease and diabetes', and gets a short answer in seconds with links to the research it used. It is free for verified US health workers. The company makes money by showing ads from drug and device companies, the same way medical journals always have.

overview.whatItDoes: OpenEvidence answers medical questions for doctors. It reads trusted sources like the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) and JAMA, which it has content deals with, and writes a short answer with citations. Doctors use it between patients to check doses, guidelines and new research. It also has a note-taking tool called Visits that writes up the patient visit for the doctor.
howItWorks: A doctor signs up and verifies they are a licensed health worker, using their NPI number (a US doctor ID).
They type or speak a clinical question in plain English.
The AI searches peer-reviewed research and guidelines, not the open internet.
It gives a short answer with numbered references the doctor can click and check.
Drug and device companies pay to show ads next to relevant answers.
Visits listens to a patient visit (with consent) and drafts the clinical note.
overview.valueProposition: A fast, free, cited answer to a medical question in 10 seconds, instead of 10 minutes of searching.

steps.detail: A senior resident shows the app on rounds.
Enters email and NPI number to verify.
Types 'first-line treatment for new atrial fibrillation in elderly patient'.
Gets a summary with guideline citations.
Taps a reference to confirm it is the latest guideline.
Tells other residents, who sign up too.
Unsure about a drug dose for a patient with weak kidneys.
Asks by voice in the corridor.
Answer includes adjustment by kidney function with sources.
A relevant drug ad appears next to the answer.
Prescribes and moves to the next patient.
Uses it several times a day.

businessModel.summary: Doctors use OpenEvidence for free. Drug and medical device companies pay to show ads to them. Because users are verified doctors, each ad view is worth far more than a normal internet ad.

revenueStreams.detail: Ads shown next to related answers, sold on CPM, which means price per 1,000 ad views. Rates for doctor audiences are much higher than consumer ads.
Hospital and health system contracts for Visits or deeper integration. Size not public.

businessModel.pricing: Free for verified US health workers. Ad pricing is not public.
costDrivers: AI model costs for every question
Licensing fees to journals like NEJM and JAMA
Medical experts who check answer quality
Sales team to sell ads to pharma
businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough example: a doctor asks 5 questions a day, about 100 a month. If half show an ad and a doctor-targeted ad earns about $100 to $300 per 1,000 views, that doctor brings in about $5 to $15 a month. AI costs for 100 questions may be under $1 to $2. So each active doctor likely makes money. The big costs are journal licences and staff, which are fixed, so profit grows as more doctors use it.

howTheyGetUsers: Doctors telling other doctors, especially residents on rounds
Free price with no hospital approval needed
Press about its high scores on medical licensing exams
Brand trust from NEJM and JAMA partnerships
whatBringsUsersBack: Daily clinical questions that never stop

growth.moat: Three things make it hard to copy: exclusive journal content deals, a verified audience of doctors that pharma will pay a lot to reach, and the habit of daily use. A rival would need all three at once.

competitors.name: UpToDate (Wolters Kluwer)
competitors.positioning: The long-time paid clinical reference, written by experts, sold to hospitals.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: OpenEvidence is free, faster and conversational, while UpToDate has decades of trust and hospital contracts.

competitors.name: Doximity
competitors.positioning: The 'LinkedIn for doctors' that also sells pharma ads and now offers AI tools.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Both sell doctor ads; OpenEvidence wins on AI search quality, Doximity on its network and tools.

competitors.name: ChatGPT and general AI
competitors.positioning: General AI many doctors already use.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: OpenEvidence uses only vetted sources and cites them, which matters for trust and safety.

competitors.name: Abridge and other AI scribes
competitors.positioning: Paid AI note-taking sold to health systems.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: OpenEvidence's Visits is free and tied to its answer engine.

pmLessons: Vertical AI wins on trust. Picking only vetted sources and showing citations beat general chatbots for doctors.
The user and the payer can be different. Doctors use it free; pharma pays to reach them.
A verified audience can be worth more than a big audience.
Get into the daily workflow. A note-writer turns an occasional tool into an every-day habit.
Partnerships can be a moat. Journal deals are slow to sign and hard for rivals to copy.

interviewQuestions.question: OpenEvidence is free and ad-supported. Is that the right model for a medical AI?
interviewQuestions.hint: List pros (fast adoption, no hospital buy-in) and cons (trust, conflict of interest). Suggest guardrails like clear labels and audits, and an optional paid tier.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure whether OpenEvidence answers are good?
interviewQuestions.hint: Mix user signals (thumbs up, citation clicks), expert audits, and outcome proxies. Make wrong-answer rate a guardrail.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you take OpenEvidence to India?
interviewQuestions.hint: Talk about local guidelines, Indian drug names and prices, verification with the National Medical Commission register, and whether Indian pharma ads can pay the bills.

interviewQuestions.question: Should OpenEvidence build an AI scribe? Why?
interviewQuestions.hint: Frame it as moving from occasional search to daily workflow. Discuss competition with Abridge and risks around patient privacy.

interviewQuestions.question: How does OpenEvidence compete with UpToDate?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare price, speed, trust and distribution. Suggest where UpToDate is still stronger, like hospital contracts, and how to win those.
